Autumn 2025

Drawing pretty pictures and solving interesting problems

Prussian Bridges

Map of Konigsberg

Prussian city of Königsberg (now Kaliningrad in Russia, spanned the Pregel river. There were 7 bridges connecting two islands and the mainland. Starting at any point, is it possible to walk around the city, crossing every bridge exactly once?

Bridges

  • Euler spotted that the route taken within the landmass doesn’t matter, only the bridges crossed.
  • Smaller island connected with \(2\) bridges to each side of the river.
  • Larger island connected to each side of the river by \(1\) bridge.
  • Islands connected by one bridge.
  • Is it possible to walk around the city, crossing every bridge exactly once?

Simplified map, showing only the bridges and land-masses

Note: Euler built a mathematical model, throwing away unneccesary detail which complicates the problem.

Can you solve the 7 bridges problem?

Islands named Kneiphof and Lomse

Graphs

  • Formally: a set of objects which are related in some way.
  • Here land masses are related by bridges.

Nodes

  • Nodes (aka vertices) are the objects,
  • Here, nodes are Discworld novels.

Edges

  • Edges (aka arcs, connections, arrows) define relationsships between nodes.
  • “Wyrd Sisters” and “Equal rites” are connected by edges, being part of the Witches series,
  • However, “Thief of Time” and “Night Watch” are not (although, some might argue they should be).

Neighbours

  • Nodes that can be reached by traversing one edge.
  • I.e., directly connected to a given node.

Degrees

  • Number of neighbours of a given node
  • I.e., number of nodes reachable by one edge traversal.

Connectedness

  • So far we have looked at node-level properties, connectedness applies to the graph as a whole.
  • Nodes that you can reach by traversing one or more edges.
  • I.e., all nodes linked by edges to given node.
  • Here we have three sets of nodes which are connected (connected components).

Paths

  • Sequence of nodes, the next node in the sequence is connected to the current node by an edge.
  • Defines a journey from one node to another by means of traversing edges.
  • There is a path from “Wyrd Sisters” to “Jingo”.
  • Actually, there are multiple paths; which is the shortest?

new edge from Equal Rites to Hogfather (Unseen University) and from Thief of Time to Night Watch (time travel).

## Cycles

<div class="columns-2">
- A path (sequence of nodes) which starts and ends at the same node.
- "Night Watch", "Jingo" and "Feet of Clay" form a cycle. 
- Hamiltonian cycles are cycles that visit every node 

  - Notoriously hard ($NP$-complete)
  - Applications in logistics, network design and scheduling.

Back to Konigsberg

  • Smaller island connected with \(2\) bridges to each side of the river.
  • Larger island connected to each side of the river by \(1\) bridge.
  • Islands connected by \(1\) bridge.

Is there a path that crosses each bridge exactly once?

The thing to notice is that, to enter and leave an island by different bridges, assuming we have to cross all of them, we need an even number of bridges connected to every landmass.

Special types of graph

Weighted Graphs

  • A graph with values assigned to edges

  • These can represent anything from distance to cost to game scoring.

  • We often want to maximise or minimise the sum of edges in a path

  • What is the shortest path from \(A\) to \(D\)?

    • Direct: \(6.8\),
    • Through \(C\): \(2.5 + 3.2 = 5.7\)
    • Through \(B\): \(! + 2.7 = 3.7\)

Acyclic Graphs

  • Graphs containing no cycles

Directed Graphs

  • So far we have seen graphs where edges- can be traversed in both directions
  • Directed graphs indicate the direction of an edge.
  • Notice that \(C\) now has no outward arrows.

Trees

  • In computer science, trees grow downwards, with the root at the top.

  • Special type of directed acyclic graph:

    • one node, called the root has no incoming edges,
    • all other nodes have exactly one incoming edge, called the parent
    • nodes with no outgoing edges are called leaves.

Applications

Decision-making

  • Map out possible events, actions and outcomes.

    • State diagrams

    Aids in designing and understanding complex systems

    Graph traversal / search

    • Process of finding a given node, or visiting every node in a graph.
    • Different search algorithms visit nodes in different orders.

    DFS

    • Start with a given node.
    • Travel as far along a path as possible,
    • Backtrack until there is an edge to an unvisited node.
    • Repeat until all nodes are visited.

    BFS

    • Start with a given node.
    • Visit all its neighbours.
    • For each neighbour, repeat the process – i.e., visit all its neighbours (two steps from the start node).
    • Repeat until all nodes ale visited.

    Graph Representations

    Adjacency matrix

    • A square table of numbers
    • Position \((i,j)\) in the table represents the connection from node \(i\) to node \(j\).
    • If there is no edge between \(i\) and \(j\), then \((i,j) = 0\).
    • If there is an edge, then \((i,j) = 1\), or equal to the weight of that edge.
    • Requires \(\mathcal{O}(n^2)\) storage space (\(n\) is the number of nodes)

    - A L K B
    A 0 1 2 0
    L 1 0 1 1
    K 2 1 0 2
    B 0 1 2 0

    Adjacency (or edge) set

    • A list of pairs \((i,j)\).
    • If \((i,j)\) is in the list, then there is an edge between \(i\) and \(j\).
    • Simple representation, less easy to work with for some problems.

    • (A,L),
    • `(A,K)‘,’(A,K)’,
    • (L,K),
    • (L,B),
    • ’(K,B),(K,B)`

    Adjacency list

    • For each node \(i\) with edges leaving it,
      • Create a list \((j_1,\ldots,j_k)\) of neighbours of node \(i\).
      • Simple to code, easy to work with.
    • In some object-orientated representations, the neighbours might be node objects, but can alse just be node names.

    • A: L, K, K, B,
    • L: K, B
    • K: B, B

    Path finding and Route Planning

    Dijkstra

    • Given a weighted graph, find the shortest path from a start node to every other node.

    A star

    • Find the shortest path from a given start node to a destination.

    Travelling Salesperson

    • Find the shortest path which visits every node.
